catalog_quote: [StressTyp2 passage 1967, Hayes 1995:211-215] Alternating stress is assigned from left-to-right, stressless first CV: and CVC heavy, CV light. Main stress is on the rightmost non-final stress. Since the strong vowels that lack main stress resist reduction processes, it is plausible to assume secondary stress ... [Hagstrom ROA-219] In Unami Delaware (Goddard 1979:21), vowels are “automatically strong” if they are long, if they occur before consonant clusters, and when they occur in even-numbered positions (counting left-to-right) in a sequence of syllables headed by underlyingly short vowels followed by a single consonant. Stress appears on the penultimate strong vowel. ... [Wikipedia, citing Goddard 1979:21,130] Long vowels and vowels before consonant clusters are automatically strong. ... some short vowels are strong even in a weakening environment; such exceptions are often marked with a gra…

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: every carried segment in the record is verbatim in held files (StressTyp2 dump in, Hagstrom excerpt, Wikipedia wikitext), but all are second-hand carriers of Goddard 1979, which we do not hold, and the record itself flags this. The carriers (Hayes via StressTyp2, Hagstrom, Wikipedia, plus Google Books snippets of Hayes quoting Goddard 1979:xi, Milligan 2005 and Rivista di Linguistica, and the Lenape Talking Dictionary's 'stress on the next to last vowel' fetched sources now) agree on a weight-sensitive right-edge system (rightmost non-final strong vowel; long V and pre-cluster V strong; even-numbered short vowels strong counting L->R), so nothing suggests the 'weight / right / CVV+CVC' coding is wrong. But the best available description, Goddard 2021 A Grammar of Southern Unami Delaware (226 pp reference grammar), and the 1979 primary are both unheld and print-only; Goddard 198
